https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Frankfurt airport halts flights after climate activists block runways
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.subtitle: Germany’s busiest hub forced to suspend operations for three hours after demonstrators glued themselves to the tarmac
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Frankfurt airport, the busiest in Germany, suspended flights for three hours on Thursday morning after climate activists blocked runways by gluing themselves to the tarmac.
The Last Generation group said in a statement that six protesters had cut through a fence and had reached various points on the runways, carrying posters reading “oil kills”.
Photographs released by the group showed protesters in orange safety vests with their hands glued to the tarmac. They were later removed from the tarmac and arrested.
Flights resumed shortly before 8am local time, about three hours after the activists started their protests. About 140 of the 1,400 flights scheduled for Thursday had to be cancelled, the airport operator Fraport said. More delays are possible during the rest of the day.
“The perpetrators face severe penalties. Their actions not only jeopardise air traffic but also human lives,” a spokesman said.
Demonstrators delayed and cancelled flights across Europe on Wednesday in a wave of protests at airports from Oslo to Barcelona, disrupting holiday getaways. Ten people were arrested at Heathrow, and Cologne-Bonn airport had to suspend flights for several hours.
Last Generation warned on Wednesday that more airports in Germany and internationally would be targeted. The group demanded that fossil fuels be phased out by 2030.
The head of the German police trade union, Andreas Rosskopf, said that legislation was needed requiring all German airports to tighten their perimeter security. “Camera technology, motion detectors, fences that are difficult to overcome or penetrate. We are appealing to the politicians responsible to immediately tighten up the Aviation Security Act. We are talking about critical infrastructure here,” he told the German tabloid Bild.
Ronja Kuenkler, a Last Generation activist, told the media that Wednesday’s protest had been only the beginning, but declined to say whether the Paris Olympics, which start on Friday, would be targeted.
The German federal police, which is in charge of border security, plans to increase its presence at big airports in response to the protests, it was reported on Thursday.

image.caption: A German police union has said that laws are needed to tighten security at big airports
The activists have been warned they face severe penalties for the protest
A protester from Last Generation sits with his hand glued to a runway and sign saying “oil kills”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Get your coffee requests in — the chancellor’s buying*
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Steve Reed Hi Rachel, lovely to see you in cabinet. Blue really suits you. Just wondering if you’re free for a budget chinwag. As secretary of state for environment, food and rural affairs, I’m hoping we can discuss my plans for environment, food and rural affairs? I know the £28 billion is probably still off the table, but these onshore wind farms don’t pay for themselves.
Rachel Reeves I thought that’s exactly what they did.
Reed Well, eventually, weather permitting, but still keen to discuss our bold green future.
Reeves I can do next Wednesday before PMQs.
Reed I’ll bring biscuits.
Louise Haigh Fifth female transport secretary paging first female chancellor! Ding ding! Just wondering if you’ve had a moment to think about my bus revolution. I want them to be the lifeblood of the community so I’m going to need a bigger budget. Coffee to discuss?
Reeves Do people still use buses?
Haigh Well, no. That’s the problem. For example, there is only one bus a day in Hutton-le-Hole. Can you believe that? If there were 20, no one would need to drive. Vive la bus revolution!
Reeves OK, fine, but stop saying revolution. We’ve changed as a party. I can do next Wednesday before PMQs.
Haigh Great, I’ll bring biscuits.
John Healey Hi Rachel, don’t know if you forgot but we were supposed to have a coffee this morning to discuss the defence budget. I brought biscuits.
Reeves Sorry, John, thought I’d messaged you. Sore throat. Can we raincheck to next Wednesday before PMQs?
Healey OK, sure, I’ll tell the generals, but Volodymyr and I were talking in Kyiv and he really needs our support.
Lisa Nandy We’ve done the costings for the Royal Opera House and it needs £800 million. Something to do with a new café and an outreach programme.
Reeves £800 million?!?
Nandy They’ve got amazing almond croissants.
Reeves Let’s discuss on Wednesday before PMQs.
James Timpson Hi Rachel, afraid we need more in the prisons budget.
Reeves OK. We can discuss next week.
Timpson Let me guess … on Wednesday before PMQs?
Wes Streeting Can we meet to discuss the budget for my AI super-surgeon plan? Transformers: Robots in Guy’s (Hospital) ;)
Reeves I don’t get it.
Streeting The strapline’s a work in progress but it will be revolutionary.
Reeves Don’t say revolutionary. We’ve changed as a party. How did it go with the junior doctors?
Streeting Great. As a sign of goodwill, they’ll accept 34.5 per cent.
Reeves OK, let’s discuss before PMQs on Wednesday.
Reeves Hi Keir, I was hoping to be in the chamber for PMQs today but I’ve got a sore throat. If anyone asks, can you let them know I’m off today?
Keir Starmer Of course. Get better soon. We need to discuss my plans for taking back our streets and breaking down barriers to opportunity and housing. Also, the wallpaper in No 11 is awful.
Reeves Coffee before PMQs next Wednesday?

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/golf/arti.title: ‘I was best in world, I had too much control…  then I changed my swing’
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/golf/arti.text:
The deranged lengths to which professional golfers will pursue perfection should never be knowingly underestimated.
Viktor Hovland was in a phenomenal vein of form towards the end of last year when he won the season-ending Tour Championship and then headed to Rome. Once plagued by his short game, the Norwegian’s chip-in at the first hole on Friday morning set the tone for the Ryder Cup and a record-breaking 9&7 victory with Ludvig Aberg over Scottie Scheffler and Brooks Koepka in the foursomes the following day was essentially the death knell. “The way I’ve played over the last couple of months, I would say I believe I am [the best player in the world],” Hovland said — not unjustly — shortly after winning 3½ points.
But then he did something almost incomprehensible. In November, Hovland called his gregarious coach, Joseph Mayo, and abruptly sacked him. He started trialling different instructors and delved into the wormhole of swing mechanics. “It sounds stupid to say, but I just felt like I had a little too much control of it,” Hovland says. “It was too dependent, for example, on my short game being really good or timing. I felt I had a more repeatable pattern a couple of years prior. I’m a very curious guy. For my own sake, I wanted to know what’s on the other side.”
The results drove Hovland to a state of furious despair. After two wins in his last five starts in 2023, he failed to finish inside the top ten once in as many events after the turn of the year. Then came the Masters, where he missed the cut after a nine-over-par second round of 81 and subsequently withdrew from the $20million RBC Heritage event the following week.
“The worst feeling is when you’re in a bad place and you don’t know how to get out of it,” Hovland says. “I was trying a bunch of stuff that just wasn’t working and it’s just miserable when you work so hard and don’t see the results. Then it’s the thoughts of, ‘Why do I even try?’ You sort of enter a bad frame of mind where it’s just like, ‘What’s the point of playing?’ I can enter a tournament and scrape by but that’s not why I play the game. I want to play at the level I know I can. If I am just here to try and make the cut, I’d rather be doing something else.”
Hovland almost withdrew from the US PGA Championship, but a third-place finish was a merciful breakthrough. He had reunited with Mayo by then, too, and the pair worked deep into dusk on the range here on Monday evening at the Renaissance Club. “We’re just trying to get better and back to where we were,” Hovland says. It might seem like a futile experiment gone wrong, but that disregards the fact that a relentless inquisitiveness has defined both the 26-year-old’s success and character far more than natural talent ever since he was child.
Hovland famously spent the winters in Oslo bashing balls into a net inside a converted aircraft hangar until his hands turned blue from blood blisters rather than the cold, but the confines of 19 hours of daily darkness fostered a thirst for stimulation. In golf terms, it meant studying kinematics, watching countless YouTube videos, and sending videos of his swing to Kelvin Miyahira, a little-known instructor in Hawaii, constantly tweaking his teenage technique. “I was never the best at anything when I was younger. I always had to turn over every single stone,” says Hovland, who was only recruited by Oklahoma State University’s prestigious golf programme in 2013 because the coaches had been scouting fellow Norwegian Kristoffer Ventura.
Beyond sport, it continues to fuel Hovland’s interest in poker, science, and even the odd conspiracy theory. “It’s like, what is the deal with all the aliens? There seem to be some pilots and commanders that explain what they saw and have video footage of it, so it’s like, ‘Huh, what is that?’ ” Hovland says. “I find the reluctance to talk about that stuff fascinating. The conspiracy is one thing but then also the reaction to it. What do you think happens after we die? We don’t know. The establishment will say, ‘Your neurons will stop firing. Your body will rot.’ OK, that’s one explanation but, if you look at our ancestors, there’s a huge culture that goes into preparing for the afterlife. Were they just idiots or were they onto something? I’m just curious to find out. We’ve gotten sold that we have all the answers but there’s just so much we don’t know. I find those questions super motivating and I just want to figure it out.”
Hovland adopted that approach in more practical terms when LIV pursued him last year following the Ryder Cup, and he concedes he instructed his agent to gather all the information about a deal to join Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton in defecting. “If I’m going to say no to something, I want to at least know what it is,” Hovland says before lamenting the PGA Tour’s “big mistake” of not doing the same when first approached by the Saudis.
“A lot of the players I’ve talked to want more transparency. And if you claim you’re representing our best interests, you at least meet with the people involved. Now we’re in this stalemate or whatever you want to call it, but it’s not something that required the prediction of 20 different chess moves.”
“I have no hard feelings against the guys that went. I completely understand because there are a lot of grey areas at the moment but, for me, I did not think their product was appealing enough to go. Obviously, they’re throwing out a lot of money, but I’ve already made a lot of money [Hovland earned more than £25million on the PGA Tour last year alone]. I’m not a very materialistic person. It’s nice to make life easier for yourself, but that’s not what gets me up in the morning.
“At the end of the day, the question is ‘What’s going to make me a better player?’ And hey, in 20 years, if I’m on the back end of my career, playing LIV Golf wouldn’t be too bad. It might have been a pretty cool opportunity but, right now, it’s something I think I’d probably look back [on] and regret.”
That question seems to govern every aspect of Hovland’s life, be it his practice routines, fitness regime, or the diet that has transformed him into a six-times PGA Tour winner — vodka soda is his drink of choice on the rare occasions he consumes alcohol. “I’m probably a tough person to truly get to know,” he says of his search for a girlfriend. “It takes time to spend with me and I haven’t given enough to do that.” But it is also why he will be among the favourites at Royal Troon next week in spite of his recent tumult and is arguably the best current player yet to win a major.
Hovland’s best opportunity was perhaps at St Andrews in 2022, when he played alongside Rory McIlroy in the final group but went on to shoot 74. For some, the reputation can be like a millstone — Xander Schauffele admitted as much after his victory at the US PGA Championship — but he is still only 26 and just five years into his pro career.
“I take it as a compliment,” Hovland says. “It’s cool if people think I deserve one, whatever that means. I’ve obviously had a few close goes but, to be fair, those don’t bother me as much as they would other people because I believe in what I’m doing and that I’m good enough to get one done, but it’s not something I’m losing sleep over.”
And you get the sense the racing mind that broke and rebuilt his swing this winter might already have enough to keep him occupied. “I’m not a guy that just wants to blindly follow people and be told what to do,” he says. “I want to understand everything.”
FedExCup Champion Viktor Hovland took time out of his busy practice schedule while in North Berwick, Scotland for the Genesis Scottish Open to surprise 11 children from the West Links Junior Golf Club at North Berwick Golf Club.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.title: Buckingham Palace’s East Wing opens its doors to the public for first time
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.subtitle: The East Wing opens for a trial period over the summer, offering a glimpse into the palace’s 19th-century fascination with Asian art
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.text:
Who could resist a peek behind the most famous net curtains in the country?
The rooms leading to the balcony of Buckingham Palace have always been off-limits to the general public.
The Royal family has traditionally preferred to wave down at them from a distance when it comes to the big balcony state occasions, but on Thursday, for the first time, visitors will have their own chance to see the balcony from the other side of those net curtains, as the East Wing opens for a trial period over the summer.
If you’re not among the 6,000 royalists who have already snapped up all the tickets within six hours of them going on sale, or you’d prefer not to pay £75 for the privilege, here’s what you’re missing.
First: the unexpected volume of Chinese-themed bling. When the royal family retire from their public appearances on the balcony, it is not immediately obvious that they are stepping back inside the Orientalist fantasy of a dissolute reprobate.
History may have remembered the reckless and reviled Prince Regent, later George IV, as “a bad son, a bad husband, a bad father, a bad subject, a bad monarch and a bad friend” but his appetite for laudanum and marrying women in secret was matched only by his enthusiasm for blowing a fortune on art and antiques. “Oriental” art, in particular.
European imitations of Asian arts and crafts were all the rage during his Regency heyday and two centuries — and one very expensive palace renovation — later, Buckingham Palace is still groaning with it.
The East Wing is open to visitors following a five-year renovation as part of the “reservicing” of Buckingham Palace. The ten-year programme, which involves everything from rewiring the building to replacing old boilers and installing new lifts, is costing the Treasury £396 million.
Visitors will find a palace of two halves, a royal headquarters full of treasures which, depending on which red-carpeted corridor you take, can feel more like a conference centre that has seen better days. Think less Versailles, more that Bournemouth hotel where Roald Dahl set The Witches.
It was the sale of George IV’s Royal Pavilion in Brighton that funded the construction of the famous palace façade we know today. Queen Victoria wanted a new wing for her expanding family and once it was built, she filled it with art and furniture from her profligate uncle’s seaside pleasure palace.
Today, George IV’s extravagant stamp is still felt strongly throughout the newly refurbished rooms, from the huge pair of porcelain pagodas, brought back from the Far East by a ship’s surgeon and which now stand at the mirrored end of the main corridor, to the absurdly camp palm tree curtain poles of the Yellow Drawing room, where the late Queen Elizabeth used to sit for official portraits.
A highlight of the tour will be entering the inner sanctum of the “Centre Room” where the royals gather before stepping out onto the balcony.
The first surprise is just how low the balustrade is. (Honestly, it is not much higher than knee-height and is the least child-friendly balcony I’ve ever seen. It is no surprise that visitors will not be allowed to step out onto it during tours; the risk of people toppling over the edge while taking selfies would be high.)
The second surprise is the Chinese theme that runs throughout the decor. They have really gone to town. Four huge tapestries, depicting caricatures of Asian figures, adorn the wall. Oriental vases stand between the double doors. A massive pink and green lotus flower chandelier which would not look out of place in a Disneyland hotel, dominates the room. And so it continues throughout the wing. Hand-painted wallpaper. Silk wall hangings. Gilt dragons. Lacquered cabinets.
I lost count of the fat Buddhas and “China man” ornaments which might be considered dangerously bad taste if encountered at a car boot sale anywhere else.
It’s a fascinating glimpse into the 19th-century fad for “Chinoiserie” but one wonders what visitors like the Emperor of Japan made of all the caricatured Asian figures adorning every other Buckingham Palace lamp base and fireplace, during his recent state visit.
A spokeswoman for the Royal Collection Trust said that the tour guides will be discussing the cultural baggage around these issues, as they lead small groups of 20 people around the rooms.
“Some of the works on display in the East Wing reflect this fascination with East Asia, and its status as an emblem of taste — even while revealing the limits of British understanding at the time,” she said.
“The wardens will be providing some of this context when talking about the objects on display.”
Ticket-holders will also be able to see the recently unveiled portrait of King Charles by Jonathan Yeo, as it commands centre stage in the ballroom.
Caroline de Guitaut, Surveyor of the King’s Works of Art, said that visitors may be surprised to see “these works that speak very loudly of George IV’s more exuberant and exotic tastes.”
She added: “It was Prince Albert’s idea to have a balcony at Buckingham Palace, because he saw it as a way of enabling the royal family to connect with the people, and of course that’s exactly how, in a sense, it continues to be used on important occasions.
“But it began to be used very early on in Queen Victoria’s reign, from 1851 waving off the troops to the Crimean War and welcoming them back on their return.”
The King was said to have been instrumental in opening up the east wing for the first time and almost 6,000 tickets were sold out within hours of going on sale in April.
The reservicing is due to be completed by 2027.

image.caption: An oriental theme runs through the decor
The new potrait of King Charles by Jonathan Yeo is on display in the ballroom
The East Wing, which leads onto the palace balcony, is opening to the public for the first time after lengthy preparations

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Theatre under fire for hosting comedian who supported Baillie Gifford boycott
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.subtitle: Royal Lyceum Theatre in Edinburgh will hold show by Nish Kumar even though its director criticised protests about the firm’s funding for the arts
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
A theatre in Edinburgh has come under fire for hosting a comedian who supported the Baillie Gifford boycott — after the venue’s boss publicly criticised the protest.
David Greig, artistic director of The Royal Lyceum, expressed support for the investment firm’s sponsorship of Scottish book festivals during protests against its involvement with Scottish book festivals.
Activist groups targeted Baillie Gifford, demanding it should divest from literary festivals owing to its investment in fossil fuels and in tech companies that operate in Israel.
Kumar waded into the controversy when he and Charlotte Church pulled out of their appearances at Hay Festival in Wales.
The comedian shared a statement from Fossil Free Books, the group that led the protests, and wrote: “Sad to say that I will be pulling out of Hay to support this campaign. Love the festival and the people that work in it, but this was the right decision for me.”
He is now set to appear at the Lyceum in September to perform his show Nish, Don’t Kill My Vibe.
When Edinburgh International Book Festival announced an abrupt end to its 20-year sponsorship deal with the asset management company, Greig said it was “irresponsible, entitled and childish” to turn down money on “pretty spurious grounds”.
“I’m worried about it. Audiences and arts organisations do not exist and cannot exist to conform to the given whims of any particular artists or sets of artists at any particular time,” he added.
While Fossil Free Books claimed that “a literary industry free from fossil fuels, genocide and colonial violence is possible and it is necessary”, another 70 Scottish writers signed an open letter calling the campaign against Baillie Gifford “deeply retrograde”.
After the partnership’s end, Allan Little, the chairman of Edinburgh International Book Festival, said that funding for the arts was in a “perilous position” and that without the support of partners and donors, the future of such festivals would be “in jeopardy”.
Baillie Gifford later pulled out of funding all UK literary festivals.
In July, nine festivals that lost Baillie Gifford’s funding issued a joint request for donations, citing “intense discussion around arts funding and challenges”.
Little also said his team could not deliver a “safe and sustainable festival” under “the constant threat of disruption from activists”.
David Black, a businessman in Edinburgh, has also questioned the theatre’s decision to host Kumar.
He said the comedian bore “a clear responsibility for the attack on those literary festivals which have benefited from the generosity of Baillie Gifford over the years”, and believes hosting Kumar could expose the theatre to protests from those who disagreed with the boycott.
Black added: “The fact that I share many of his underlying values as far as Palestine and fossil fuels are concerned is not the issue here.
“It is a matter of the potential risk to patrons and staff of the Royal Lyceum Theatre. This should be a priority concern of the management and the funding owners, the local authority.
“Don’t Kill my Vibe should be pulled without delay.”
The Lyceum declined to comment. Nish Kumar’s representative has been approached for comment.

image.caption: The Royal Lyceum Theatre will host Nish, Don’t Kill My Vibe
Extinction Rebellion activists block the entrance to Baillie Gifford’s headquarters calling for it to divest from fossil fuels
Kumar waded into the controversy about arts funding when he pulled out of a gig at the Hay Festival
